ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

shoulder imaging — clinical pattern 5

An older woman has shoulder pain after a low-energy fall. Imaging shows a fracture below the humeral tuberosities with shaft angulation, while the humeral head remains seated in the glenoid. The AC joint is aligned. Which injury accounts for the radiographic abnormality?

  1. Proximal humeral surgical-neck fracture
  2. Anterior glenohumeral dislocation
  3. Posterior glenohumeral dislocation
  4. Inferior glenohumeral dislocation
  5. Acromioclavicular separation
Answer and explanation

Proximal humeral surgical-neck fracture

A fracture below the tuberosities separates the shaft from the proximal humeral segment.

Option explanations

Proximal humeral surgical-neck fracture: A fracture below the tuberosities separates the shaft from the proximal humeral segment.

Anterior glenohumeral dislocation: The humeral head lies anterior to the glenoid, commonly in a subcoracoid position. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Posterior glenohumeral dislocation: Axillary or another appropriate orthogonal view shows the humeral head behind the glenoid; AP imaging alone may miss it. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Inferior glenohumeral dislocation: The humeral head lies below the glenoid, often with the arm fixed overhead. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Acromioclavicular separation: The distal clavicle is displaced relative to the acromion while the glenohumeral joint remains located. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
